item.title: Photo ZIP campaign targeting hospitality industry delivers Node.js implant for persistent access
item.description:
Unattributed campaign active since April 2026 targets European and Asian hospitality orgs with a TonRAT Node.js implant, routing phishing through Calendly and Google to pass SPF/DKIM/DMARC checks clean.
- Delivery uses photo-themed ZIP archives containing fake LNK files (IMG-/PHOTO-*.png.lnk, 1,989-2,079 bytes) dropped via browser download. Phishing emails sent through a threat-actor-controlled Calendly account (em1618.calendly[.]com) pass all email auth checks, a technique Microsoft calls "authentication laundering." A four-hop redirect chain (Calendly -> share[.]google -> google[.]com -> photo-*[.]cfd) fragments URL reputation before serving the ZIP behind a Cloudflare Turnstile gate.
- The attack chain: LNK spawns obfuscated PowerShell using BigInt arithmetic (7 documented phases, XOR through for-loop variants) to download a .ps1 from photo-*.cfd domains. Wave 2 adds csc.exe -> cvtres.exe dynamic .NET DLL compilation before deploying node.exe (v24.13.0, SHA-256: d14ba95c...) from AppData\Local\Nodejs\ to run randomly named .js payloads with C2 domains as arguments (safedocphoto[.]info, recallnine[.]info, kentjerk[.]info).
- Persistence is dual and self-healing: HKCU\Run keeps Node.js alive; HKCU\RunOnce points to a ProgramData EXE that refreshes the RunOnce entry after each execution, creating a loop. Defender blocked PE payload xmnrwv9l.exe (04ec44f2...) via Wacatac, but the Node.js Run key survived and resumed C2 two days later.

item.title: Zero-Day Exploitation of Vulnerability (CVE-2026-20245) in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager
item.description:
CVE-2026-20245 zero-day in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager exploited in the wild: attackers escalated from admin SSH to root via malicious CSV upload, then ran a cleanup script to erase their tracks.
Key findings:
- Initial access began as early as late 2025 via rogue SD-WAN peering connections, possibly exploiting CVE-2026-20127 or CVE-2026-20182 (both critical auth-bypass flaws in the peering mechanism). By March 2026 the actor authenticated over SSH as vmanage-admin, changed the default admin account password to access the web UI, exfiltrated SD-WAN fabric configs via /dataservice/ REST endpoints, then quietly reverted the password to avoid alerting operators.
- CVE-2026-20245 lives in the CLI tenant-upload feature, which fails to sanitize uploaded file content. The actor ran: request tenant-upload tenant-list /home/admin/evil_tenant.csv vpn 0. The payload appended a backdoor account named troot (UID 0) to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, then the actor switched to it via su. Full root achieved from a standard admin session.
- Anti-forensics were deliberate and scripted. The actor deleted evil_tenant.csv, restored vbond_vsmart_tenant_list and the original passwd/shadow backups, then ran a validation script confirming every indicator read ABSENT before disconnecting. Disk artifacts may be gone, but log artifacts survive.

item.title: Analyzing Active Exploitation of Lantronix and OpenWRT LuCI
item.description:
CVE-2025-67038, an unauthenticated OS command injection in Lantronix EDS5000 serial-to-IP converters, was exploited in the wild before public disclosure, suggesting patch-diff reverse engineering by a targeted threat cluster.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-67038 lives in OpenWRT LuCI's HTTP JSON-RPC auth endpoint. The username field in /cgi-bin/luci/rpc/auth is concatenated unsanitized into a log string passed to os.execute, allowing root command execution with no credentials. Exploitation probes injected sleep tests then capability-check callbacks to C2s at 154.219.113[.]56 and 38.180.201[.]49, with filenames like lntxe1-lntxea confirming the actor knew exactly what device they were hitting.
- The cluster, named Chaya_006, operated April 5 to June 3 from scanner IPs across Asia (Japan 🇯🇵, Taiwan 🇹🇼, South Korea 🇰🇷, China 🇨🇳). Scanner IPs include 38.207.136[.]2 and 59.124.166[.]52. The actor rotated user-agents from curl to Chrome to Firefox to blend in, a deliberate evasion step, not scanner noise.
- Parallel to Chaya_006, over 4,100 brute-force attempts hit OpenWRT LuCI /cgi-bin/luci/ endpoints between January and June, cycling hundreds of password combinations across four usernames. Nearly 32,000 LuCI-exposed devices are visible on Shodan today.
Hunt for POST requests to /cgi-bin/luci/rpc/auth containing shell metacharacters in the username parameter, and alert on outbound wget/curl/nslookup from OT-adjacent serial converter devices.

item.title: STOCKSTAY Another Day: The Latest Addition to Turla’s Intelligence Gathering Apparatus
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 FSB-linked Turla deploys STOCKSTAY, a new .NET backdoor active since December 2022, targeting Ukrainian 🇺🇦 government and military networks alongside European foreign affairs entities.
- STOCKSTAY is a multi-component .NET backdoor split across three roles mirroring KAZUAR's architecture: STOCKBROKER (tunneler, C2 via WebSocket), STOCKMARKET (orchestrator), and STOCKTRADER (backdoor execution: file ops, registry R/W, command execution). Persistence is set via HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, with components installed under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\SMN\. Config files disguise themselves as cryptocurrency app JSON, embedding encrypted C2 details inside fake trading service fields.
- Initial access spans malicious RDP files, phishing with academic and diplomatic lures, a WinRAR path traversal (CVE-2025-8088), and malicious HTA files. STOCKSTAY.MARKETMAKER masquerades as "MicrosoftUpdateOneDrive" and pulls component ZIPs from compromised WordPress sites and Ukrainian 🇺🇦 government infrastructure.
- Environmental keying is a core evasion technique: config decryption requires the target hostname, username, or domain, making sandbox analysis fail silently. C2 operates via wss:// WebSocket to Render-hosted servers including wss://driverx86-adobe.onrender[.]com/ws and wss://google-ai-labs-it.onrender[.]com/ws, active Monday-Friday 0900-1800 to blend with business traffic.

item.title: From Code to Coverage (Part 6): What netlogon.log Sees That Event 1644 Never Will
item.description:
ldapnomnom's README claims "no Windows audit logs generated." Source code and lab testing say otherwise: the tool uses TCP, not UDP, making Event 5156 a reliable detection source most orgs are not collecting.
Key findings:
- ldapnomnom sends LDAP Ping requests (NtVer + AAC + User filter, NetLogon attribute, base-scope rootDSE) over TCP, not true UDP cLDAP. The cldap:// UDP path exists in the underlying lkarlslund/ldap library but ldapnomnom never calls DialURL. Every connection is ldap.Dial("tcp", ...). Event 5156 fires for every connection with full source IP, LSASS.exe as the application, and Protocol 6 (TCP) confirmed. The README is wrong in a way that benefits defenders.
- Event 1644 is structurally blind to LDAP Ping regardless of threshold settings. The NtVer+AAC+User filter is dispatched by LSASS to the netlogon.dll handler before the LDAP engine is involved. No registry key or verbosity setting changes this. Zero Event 1644 entries in lab testing across 40 usernames.
- Enable nltest /dbflag:0x2080ffff and netlogon.log captures every queried username and the defender-only third state: a [MISC] NlSamVerifyUserAccountEnabled line appears for disabled accounts before Sam User Unknown Ex. The attacker sees identical misses for disabled and nonexistent accounts. The DC and the log do not. Source IP shows (null) in all cases.
- True UDP cLDAP (cldap_ping.py, any tool calling cldap://) eliminates Event 5156 entirely.

item.title: From San Pedro to Salinas: How a Chinese Framework “DCloud Uni-App” Powers a Global Scam Economy
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 open-source framework DCloud Uni-App underpins 236,000+ scam domains globally, from Argentine crypto fraud to active U.S. 🇺🇸 investment scams with real FinCEN registrations.
Key findings:
- DCloud Uni-App leaves recognizable fingerprints: default scaffolding paths, a characteristic AndroidManifest package convention (uni.UNIxxxxxxx), and io.DCloud.application.DCloudApplication as the application class. These fingerprints link rainbowex[.]cc, lsscol[.]com, ystl03106[.]top, and 236,000+ other scam domains to a shared build pipeline. Evasive operators strip the defaults but retain scam-specific template strings, and they run bulletproof hosting at double the rate (14-17% vs 5-10%), centering on AS152194 CTG Server Limited.
- The LSSC scooter scam (lsscol[.]com, lsscapp[.]com, lightacer[.]com) caused millions in U.S. 🇺🇸 losses across 20 states before collapsing in August 2025. Its Android app, decompiled by Yale Privacy Lab, confirmed the full DCloud stack alongside Chinese 🇨🇳 tech references (QQ, Taobao, Alibaba).
- Yuechi Sharing Technology Ltd. (ystl03106[.]top) is active now, targeting U.S. 🇺🇸, Australian 🇦🇺, and New Zealand victims. It holds a real FinCEN MSB registration (No. 31000300306222) and Hong Kong incorporation as legitimacy props. The shared customer-service chat backend ties it to XAEL-AI (xaai3xj[.]com, xaaitbb[.]com), indicating centralized operator infrastructure.

item.title: Introduction to COM usage by Windows threats
item.description:
COM abuse is a persistent blind spot in triage: Qakbot, Attor, WarmCookie, and Gh0stRAT all weaponize Windows COM interfaces to hide behavior behind vtable indirection, evade EDR telemetry, and achieve persistence without touching schtasks.exe.
Key findings:
- COM hides attacker intent behind indirect vtable calls like "call qword ptr [rax+38h]". Until you recover the interface type and apply it in IDA or Binary Ninja, WMI access, BITS transfers, and scheduled task creation are invisible. Qakbot uses CoInitializeSecurity then CoCreateInstance with IID_IWbemLocator to reach WMI. Attor uses IBackgroundCopyJob for C2 and exfiltration over BITS, the same service Windows Update uses.
- Gh0stRAT and WarmCookie both create scheduled tasks entirely through COM (Task Scheduler 2.0 CLSID {0F87369F-A4E5-4CFC-BD3E-73E6154572DD} or the older CLSID_CTaskScheduler), never spawning schtasks.exe. That means process-creation telemetry alone misses the persistence event.
- DCOM lateral movement (T1021.003) is fingerprinted by CoCreateInstanceEx with remote COSERVERINFO parameters. CoInitializeSecurity and CoSetProxyBlanket calls signal the sample is configuring impersonation for out-of-process or remote COM use.
Takeaway: In IDA, apply ITaskServiceVtbl, IWbemLocatorVtbl, or IBackgroundCopyJobVtbl to recovered interface pointers, then use the COM Helper plugin or COMIDA to rename GUID references.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2070085579971101123

item.title: Your Endpoints Are Running Local AI Agents — Can You See Them?
item.description:
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint now inventories local AI agents on Windows and macOS, giving responders a hunting surface for tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Ollama that execute with user-level permissions and may reach files, commands, and external MCP servers.
Key findings:
- MDE discovers supported local agents automatically: CLI tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI), desktop apps (ChatGPT Desktop, Ollama, Perplexity), agentic IDEs (Cursor, Kiro, Devin), VS Code extensions (Cline, Roo Code), and Claw-based agents. Data surfaces in Advanced Hunting via the AIAgentsInfo table (renaming to AgentsInfo on July 1, 2026, API callers must update).
- Each record exposes RelatedProcess (e.g., code.exe), TrustedProcess, AccountName, AccountSid, DeviceName, IsBlocked, Scope, and AgentCreationTime. SID is more reliably populated than account name, so SID-based pivots are more durable during IR.
- During incident response, filter by compromised account or device: add "where AccountName contains" or swap in AccountSid to surface every agent tied to that identity, its publishing status, and which device it ran on.
Practitioner takeaway: run AIAgentsInfo | where Platform == "LocalAgents" | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by AIAgentId to get a deduplicated current-state inventory. Flag devices with five or more agents and any agent where IsBlocked == false but Scope == tenant-wide as priority review items.

item.title: AI Security Incident Case: Jetbrains Plugin Supply Chain Attack Stealing AI Key
item.description:
15 malicious JetBrains plugins with ~70,000 installs silently exfiltrated AI API keys to an attacker-controlled server, forming an underground key-resale economy active since October 2025.
Key findings:
- All 15 plugins share one codebase, repackaged under 7 vendor accounts. They pose as DeepSeek/OpenAI tools (code completion, Git commits, bug detection). The save() method triggers on "Apply", verifies the key format (sk-, 51 chars), then calls BaseUtil.request() to POST the key to 39.107.60[.]51 via plaintext HTTP with static auth token F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D. No prompt, no async delay, invisible to the user.
- Attackers merged the exfil call directly into normal configuration persistence logic, the primary technique for passing manual JetBrains marketplace review. Plaintext HTTP means any intermediate device on a corporate intranet or VPN can capture the key in transit.
- The business model is a closed loop: stolen keys are pooled server-side, then sold as "AI compute access" to paying users. Keys issued to paying customers are almost certainly other victims' credentials.
- IDE plugins run unsandboxed with full filesystem and network access, making them high-value supply chain targets. The same attack pattern has appeared in VS Code (GlassWorm).
Hunt for outbound HTTP POST connections from JetBrains processes (idea.exe, goland.exe, etc.) to direct IPs.

item.title: ESET takes part in Operation Endgame to disrupt Amadey and Stealc
item.description:
Operation Endgame dismantles Amadey and Stealc MaaS infrastructure, taking down roughly 50 domains and nearly 200 active C&C IPs used by affiliates of both families worldwide.
Key findings:
- ESET shared three years of tracking data covering Q4 2025 through H1 2026: C&C server lists, RC4 encryption keys, build identifiers, campaign IDs, and URL path patterns. That intelligence let law enforcement distinguish individual affiliate clusters from shared infrastructure and prioritize high-impact targets. ESET identified 53 distinct Amadey clusters and 73 Stealc clusters using graph modeling on extracted config values.
- Amadey (tracked since 2018, pay-per-rebuild at $600 + $50/build) embeds up to three C&C URLs, an RC4 key, and a six-character hex sd value per sample. The RC4 key is a reliable affiliate identifier: rebuilds rotate the sd value but preserve the key. C&C comms use HTTP POST with RC4-encrypted key-value data. Largest single cluster represented 34% of all samples and averaged 14 payloads dropped per victim, running its own pay-per-install model and overlapping with Lumma Stealer affiliates.
- Stealc (tracked since Feb 2023, $300/month subscription, now at v2.22.1) uses two separate RC4 keys per sample: one for string decryption, one for C&C traffic. C&C comms use HTTP with RC4-encrypted JSON; a session access_token and a one-time random nonce per response defeat static RC4 traffic signatures.

item.title: What do Ports Hear When Nobody's Listening? An Assessment of Automated Cybercrime [Guest Diary], (Wed, Jun 24th)
item.description:
Honeypot analysis of three IoT botnets, Terrabot, r00ts3c, and RondoDox, reveals a layered automated threat economy hitting legacy CVEs at volume while masking sophisticated fileless loaders beneath the noise.
- Terrabot (User-Agent: terrabot-owned-you) fired 24 hits from 24 unique IPs across 11 days, targeting CVE-2018-10561 (Dasan GPON) and CVE-2016-20017 (D-Link DSL) and CVE-2016-20016 (MVPower DVR JAWS RCE) via staging server hxxp://140[.]233.190.47. Most attempts were broken: GPON POST bodies were empty, and the JAWS payload was rejected with HTTP 400 because a raw unencoded space after wget+ broke the URI parser. Sloppy copy-paste scripting, but volume covers the slop.
- r00ts3c (User-Agent: r00ts3c-owned-you) ran a more deliberate campaign. It targeted CVE-2025-34037 (Linksys tmUnblock.cgi), SOAP router control endpoints, and CVE-2016-20017, pulling architecture-specific binaries (kaizen.arm, kaizen.mpsl) from staging server hxxp://176[.]65.149.168. A node at 20.210.107.25 traced to Microsoft Azure cloud infrastructure; a later hit came from 83.142.209.46 in Ukraine 🇺🇦, acting as a self-referential P2P staging node. Hard-coded Host headers (127.0.0.1:80 or a DigitalOcean IP) fingerprint the bot regardless of target.
- RondoDox is the deeper find.

item.title: Malicious Edge extension abuses Native Messaging as bridge to malware
item.description:
"Edgecution" malware abuses Chrome Native Messaging to break out of the Edge browser sandbox and deploy a Python backdoor, serving as a bridge for the Payouts Kings ransomware operation.
Key findings:
- Initial access via Microsoft Teams vishing: attackers pose as IT support and direct victims to a fake "Outlook Updates Management Console" that downloads a malformed-header ZIP, pastes clipboard scripts, or phishes M365 credentials. Three delivery options: AutoHotKey, batch script, or PowerShell.
- The ZIP contains embedded Python 3.13.3 plus extension and native directories. A scheduled task launches a headless Edge instance running the malicious extension (disguised as "Edge Monitoring Agent"), invisible to the user.
- Sandbox escape via Chrome Native Messaging: the extension invokes a batch file in the native directory, which is registered via a native messaging manifest, spawning the Python backdoor as a separate host-level process outside the browser sandbox (T1559).
- The Python backdoor accepts commands relayed from the extension: execute shell or PowerShell, run arbitrary Python, write files, enumerate processes, and gather system info. Unused commands suggest active development.
Hunt for: scheduled tasks launching msedge.exe with --headless flags, unexpected native messaging manifests under HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\NativeMessagingHosts or the Edge equivalent, and unsigned Python runtimes in user-writable directories.

item.title: I Wasted 3 Days Intercepting a Flutter App. Here’s What Actually Works.
item.description:
Flutter apps silently block proxy interception because BoringSSL bypasses Android's certificate trust chain entirely. Three days of failed attempts led to a two-script Frida solution covering every TLS validation layer at once.
Key findings:
- Flutter ships its own TLS stack via BoringSSL compiled into libflutter.so, completely ignoring Android's system CA store. Installing Burp's CA through device Settings has zero effect. ReFlutter patches only the Flutter binary and misses any Java or WebView connectivity checks that run before Dart initializes.
- disable-flutter-tls-v1.js finds ssl_verify_peer_cert in libflutter.so via byte pattern matching across arm64, arm, x64, and x86, then replaces it with a stub returning 0. A retry loop with five one-second delays handles the common silent failure where Frida attaches before libflutter.so finishes loading.
- universal_bypass.js covers the Java layer: custom X509TrustManager, SSLContext hook, HostnameVerifier, WebViewClient, and crucially InAppWebViewClient at com.pichillilorenzo.flutter_inappwebview_android.webview.in_app_webview.InAppWebViewClient. That last hook was missing from every existing script and is the reason WebView traffic stays blocked even when everything else works.
- When scripts alone are not enough: iptables DNAT redirects port 443/80 to Burp at kernel level since Flutter ignores Android proxy settings.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2069798749518328004

item.title: StealC and Amadey: Breaking down infostealers and the cybercrime services that deliver them
item.description:
Microsoft and Europol disrupt 200+ StealC and Amadey C2 domains on June 24, 2026, exposing the full MaaS infostealer pipeline from credential theft to ransomware deployment.
Key findings:
- StealC (C++) defeats Chromium App-Bound Encryption via APC injection into a suspended process, writing decrypted credentials to C:\ProgramData\<HWID>.txt before exfil. It also raids Outlook profiles under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\<version>\Outlook\Profiles, WinSCP sessions from HKCU\Software\Martin Prikryl\WinSCP 2\Sessions, and Steam files including ssfn* and loginusers.vdf. All data is RC4-encrypted and Base64-encoded before POST to C2. Self-delete fires last if the flag is set.
- Amadey (active since 2018) persists as nudwee.exe under C:\Users\<user>\e079729711 via scheduled task, communicates over HTTP with RC4+hex encoding, and supports 20+ backdoor commands including enabling RDP (fDenyTSConnections=0), creating hidden admin accounts, and loading cred.dll and clip.dll plugins at runtime.
- IOCs from the report: StealC C2 at hxxp://polse[.]us/62ea47cac2534aa18f74.php and hxxp://bluescry[.]com/01f96fd710e905ca2326.php; Amadey C2 at hxxp://microsoft-telemetry[.]at/cvdfnaFJBmC0/index.php. Full hash and URL list in the Microsoft Security blog.
Hunt for nudwee.exe, scheduled tasks pointing to the e079729711 directory, rundll32 loading cred.dll or clip.dll, and outbound HTTP POST to .php endpoints with RC4+Base64 bodies.

item.title: StrikeShark: investigating a new campaign delivering Cobalt Strike through SharkLoader
item.description:
StrikeShark: previously undocumented SharkLoader delivers Cobalt Strike Beacon across government, diplomatic, and software targets in 10+ countries. Attribution points to Chinese-speaking 🇨🇳 actors with low confidence; no known APT overlap.
Key findings:
- SharkLoader uses DLL sideloading via a copied legitimate SystemSettings.exe to load a three-stage chain: SystemSettings.dll (main loader) decrypts DscCoreR.mui with Blowfish ECB, which decrypts SyncRes.dat with AES-128, then decompresses and executes Cobalt Strike Beacon entirely in memory. MZ headers are stripped from encrypted files as an anti-analysis measure.

item.title: Testing AI Threat Hunting against Real-World KQL: A Side-by-Side Test
item.description:

Key findings:
- Both ChatGPT (GPT-5.5) and Claude (Sonnet 4.6) scoped their queries to DeviceProcessEvents alone, missing roughly 70% of telemetry. The human query searched DeviceProcessEvents AND DeviceEvents, which is where much of the PowerShell ScriptContent and ActionType telemetry lives. Querying only one table is a silent coverage gap, not a syntax error.
- ChatGPT's query failed to execute entirely due to unsupported pipe-chaining syntax. Claude's ran but returned 3 results versus 12 from the human query. A query that runs and looks reasonable is not the same as a query that hunts accurately.

- Schema awareness is the core gap. LLMs produce syntactically plausible KQL but don't know which fields carry what data in your environment. Hunting for the literal string Invoke-Mimikatz or scoping only to powershell.exe creates the illusion of coverage.
Takeaway: use LLMs to prototype and review discrete query blocks, not to own the full hunt.

item.title: Out of Shift: How a Shared State Bug in V8’s AsmJS Parser Broke the Ubercage
item.description:
CVE-2026-3542 in Chrome's V8 AsmJS parser corrupts WebAssembly opcode streams, bypassing the Ubercage sandbox entirely to reach arbitrary code execution from a single bug.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-3542, patched March 3 2026, lives in AsmJsParser::ValidateHeapAccess(). The heap_access_shift_position_ attribute is instance-level state shared across all recursive parse calls. A nested shift expression like HEAP32[1 << (n >> 2)] causes ShiftExpression() to recurse, overwriting that position with a stale offset. When DeleteCodeAfter() truncates the opcode stream using that stale value, subsequent opcodes are left misaligned and later emitted immediates become orphaned opcodes the decoder executes unchecked.
- The Ubercage bypass is structural, not incidental. AsmJS-generated opcodes skip ValidationTag::validate entirely because V8 trusts its own parser output. An attacker who controls the corrupted stream can inject opcodes like kExprCallRef or kExprStructGet with no type-safety checks, treating arbitrary 64-bit values on the stack as addresses. This gives out-of-sandbox read/write from a single memory-corruption primitive.
- Exploit chain: spray TypeDefinition structs on the canonical type zone so a cross-module struct type lands adjacent to the AsmJS module's type vector. Use kExprI64Const to place a crafted 64-bit address on the stack, then kExprStructGet/kExprStructSet for arbitrary read/write.

item.title: PixelSmash – Critical FFmpeg Vulnerability Turns Media Files into Weapons
item.description:
CVE-2026-8461 (CVSS 8.8): heap OOB write in FFmpeg's MagicYUV decoder enables RCE via a single 50 KB media file upload, hitting Jellyfin, Nextcloud, Emby, Immich, OBS, and AI/ML pipelines.
- CVE-2026-8461 lives in libavcodec/magicyuv.c. When slice_height is odd (attacker-controlled via bitstream), ceiling-rounded chroma shifts accumulate an extra row per slice past the allocated buffer. With coded_height=32 and slice_height=31, the decoder writes 640 attacker-controlled bytes one full row beyond the Cb chroma plane, landing directly on the AVBuffer struct FFmpeg allocates immediately after pixel data.
- Exploitation overwrites AVBuffer.free with system() and AVBuffer.opaque with a shell command pointer. When av_frame_unref fires during normal frame cleanup, the hijacked indirect call executes the attacker's command before the process crashes. JFrog demonstrated a reverse shell on Jellyfin 10.9 (jellyfin-ffmpeg 7.1.3) via automatic library scan and on Nextcloud via the Movie preview provider, both triggered by uploading a single crafted AVI with zero authentication. ASLR was disabled for the RCE demo; without ASLR bypass the primitive reliably delivers DoS on every tested target.
- The torrent vector is zero-click: a malicious AVI dropped into Jellyfin's watched media folder triggers ffprobe automatically.

item.title: Building a CI/CD pipeline for Sigma rules
item.description:
Detection as Code in practice: a full CI/CD pipeline for Sigma rules cuts out the "edit and save in the SIEM console" failure mode with automated validation, translation, testing, and shadow-mode deployment.
Key details:
- The four-stage pipeline is validate, translate, test, deploy. sigma-cli (wrapping pySigma) handles validation and conversion with no paid tooling. The SigmaHQ/sigma-rules-validator GitHub Action checks rules against the official JSON Schema. A 30-line Python script enforces metadata completeness: title, status, date, author, logsource, detection, and MITRE ATT&CK tags are all required or CI fails.
- Translated outputs (Sentinel KQL, Splunk SPL, Elastic Lucene) live under platform-translations/ as build artifacts generated by CI, never hand-edited. Field mapping pipelines applied at conversion time are where silent failures hide: a missing pipeline flag produces a syntactically valid query that matches nothing.
- Every rule needs two JSON fixtures: one true-positive event and one true-negative. pytest evaluates compiled queries against both. CERT-EU's droid goes further, running actual Atomic Red Team simulations in a sandbox and verifying the Sigma rule fires on real telemetry, eliminating "the fixture was wrong, not the rule" failures.
- New rules deploy to the SIEM with alerting suppressed for at least seven days (shadow mode). Match volume and event samples get human review before promotion.

Takeaway: Hunt your Entra sign-in logs for token requests to login.microsoftonline[.]com carrying brk_client_id targeting those three app IDs. item.description:

item.title: FortiBleed: Everything You Need to Know
item.description:

Key findings: - The attack is a two-stage, self-reinforcing credential stuffing operation: attackers test known breach dump and infostealer credentials against internet-facing FortiGate and SSL VPN devices, then use compromised devices as passive network traffic sniffers to harvest additional credentials fed back into the scanner. Over 2,500 devices were breached with a single default credential (admin3:123456). - CVE-2026-24858, a FortiCloud SSO SAML authentication bypass (CVSS 9.8) disclosed January 2026, has been discussed as a possible contributor to initial access in a subset of cases, but is not the primary mechanism. This is not a zero-day campaign. - The stolen database is organized by country, sector, and organization revenue, the structure of an initial access inventory staged for sale. Telecom leads by volume; government, energy, healthcare, and financials are heavily represented. India 🇮🇳 and the US 🇺🇸 account for nearly a third of all entries. - Password rotation alone is insufficient. Attackers had admin access long enough to alter configs, add accounts, or adjust monitoring settings. Those changes survive a password reset.
Treat any device in the dataset as already compromised.

item.title: FortiBleed Campaign Exposing Credentials for 73,932 FortiGate Systems
item.description:

item.title: Bleeding Out
item.description:
A well-resourced threat actor compromised 149+ Active Directory domains by using victim firewalls as passive PCAP sensors, harvesting 148,000+ Kerberos hashes and 33,000 NTLM hashes without touching internal endpoints.
Key findings: - Initial access via SSH brute-force of firewall management interfaces using default/vendor-pattern credentials, and mass SSL-VPN portal spraying. Three iterative spray series each fed recovered credentials back as wordlist input, creating a self-reinforcing loop backed by 46-GPU cracking across three platforms. - Post-access pivot uses the compromised firewall's own management API to trigger and download PCAPs of internal traffic. A custom harvester extracts auth material from 15+ protocols including Kerberos pre-auth exchanges. No implants dropped on internal hosts, leaving a near-silent footprint. - AD exploitation follows with cracked creds: enumeration, Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, delegation abuse, and file share staging. Confirmed exfiltration of classified defence documentation from a major defence electronics manufacturer elevates this beyond IAB or ransomware-precursor activity. - 7 Kali VMs auto-reinstall from cyberstrike[.]io on reboot. Decoy IPs are injected as false-flag attribution material and simultaneously act as canary validators in spray campaigns, deliberately corrupting IOC-based detection.

item.title: New Abuse of the ClickOnce Technology, Part 2: Stop Threat Actors from Clicking Once and Staying Forever
item.description:
ClickOnce weaponized for stealthy delivery, persistence, and COM hijacking. Attackers abuse Microsoft's own deployment tech to execute malware inside legitimate process trees without elevated privileges.
Key findings: - Payload runs under rundll32.exe and dfsvc.exe, legitimate Microsoft processes, giving threat actors built-in LOLBins cover. .application and .appref-ms files bypass mailbox filters and SmartScreen scrutiny that would catch a plain .exe. - The .appref-ms shortcut dropped to %Users\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\ is a persistence artifact. Place it in Startup or wire it to a scheduled task and the C2 payload silently updates every time it runs, no user prompt, no UAC, no admin rights required. - Trojanizing signed app dependencies (dependency hijacking or new deployment creation) lets attackers inherit a trusted signature without breaking it, sliding past SmartScreen entirely. - CrowdStrike identified what it believes is a new COM hijacking abuse surface discovered inside dfdll!BindToServer(), adding another vector to an already underdiscussed attack surface.
Hunt for .appref-ms files outside the Start Menu Programs path, scheduled tasks or Startup folder entries pointing to .appref-ms, and child processes of dfsvc.exe or rundll32.exe making outbound connections. Flag unsigned ClickOnce deployments and audit dependency manifests on any ClickOnce app in your environment.
